analytic.title: Response-Time Bounds of Rule-Based Programs under Rule Priority Structure *

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.head: A key index of the performance of a rule-based program used in real-time monitoring and control is its response time, defined by the maximum number of rule firings before a fixed point of the program is reached from a start state. Previous work in computing the response-time bounds f o r rule-based programs assumes that if two rules are enabled, then either one of them may be scheduled for firing. This assumption may be too conservative in the case programmers choose to impose a priority structure on the set of rules. In this paper, we discuss how to get tighter bounds by taking rule-priority information into account. We show that the rule-suppression relation we previously introduced can be extended to incorporate rule-priority information. A bound-derivation algorithm for programs whose potential-trigger relations satisfy an acyclicity condition is presented, followed by its correctness proof and an analysis example.
Introduction
div.p: In recent years, there has been increasing interest in the use of rule-based programs in time-critical applications, e.g., monitoring the engine of the Space Shuttle. In these applications, the rule-based program is often used to monitor the environment and must compute an output in response to significant changes that are observed in the environment. Such computation must be completed sufficiently fast so that the system can react to environmental changes in a predictable fashion. The verification/validation of the behavior of rule-based programs is of both practical and theoretical interest. Related work in real-time AI systems can be found in [l] [7] [lo] [9] [ 6 ] .

In [$I, the concept of a response time is defined for the equational rule-based program (EQL) by the (maximum) number of rule-firings before the program reaches a fixed point (a program state where all the program variables attain stable values). It was shown in that paper that the determination of the response time for arbitrary programs is in general undecidable, and is PSPACE-hard for finite-state programs. Recently there have been several papers presenting efficient methods of computing response-time bounds for rule-based programs [5] [4] [ll] [3]. However, none of those methods makes use of the rule-priority information in the program. Rule priority is a common feature in rule-based languages. It is used to constrain rule-firing order. With the presence of rule priorities, a program has fewer possible firing sequences, therefore possibly shorter response time, compared with the same program without rule priorities.

In this paper, we address the rule-priority issue in computing response-time bounds. We show that the rule-suppression relation we previously introduced in [ll] can be extended to incorporate rule-priority information. Since the rule-suppression relation is useful in deriving tighter bounds and rule priority can now be viewed as a form of rule suppression, making use of such information in bound derivation can result in tighter bounds. A bound-derivation algorithm is presented, followed by its correctness proof. A response-time analyzer is implemented to analyze programs whose potential-trigger relations satisfy an acyclicity relation. An analysis example is given to demonstrate the analysis process.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. The EQL language is described in Section 2, together with program state space and program execution. In Section 3 we introduce the basis of our response-time bound analysis theory and extend it to incorporate rule priority. In Section 4 we present an algorithm to compute response-time bounds for programs whose potential-trigger graphs are acyclic. We have imple-mented an analyzer based on the algorithm. An analysis example is presented in Section 5 , followed by concluding remarks and future research topics in Section 6.

div.head: The EQL language
div.p: EQL is a rule-based programming language designed for developing real-time decision systems where the set of decision variables is fixed a priori [2]. This seems to be the claas of rule-based programs that are most commonly found in real-time expert system applications. An EQL program consists of a finite set of rules each of which is of the form:
div.formula: priority v1 := el ! w2 := e2 ! ... ! v , := e, IF test
div.p: where priorityis an optional specification for the rule's priority (default 0), ei is an integer expression whose value is to be assigned to variable wi when the rule fires, m 2 1, and test is a predicate on the variables in the program. A rule has three parts:
1. VAR: the left-hand-side variables of the multiple assignment statement, 2. VAL: the right-hand-side expressions of the multiple assignment statement, and 3. EC: the enabling condition.

A rule is enabled at some instant if its test is evaluated to true according to the values of its variables at that moment, otherwise it is disabled. A rule is conflictive at some instant if any of its VAR variable is not equal to the corresponding VAL expression. A rule firing is the execution of the multiple assignment statement, which consists of the evaluation of all the VAL expressions, followed by updating the VAR variables with the valum of the corresponding expressions.
A rule is fimbk iff it is enabled and conflictive.

An execution of an EQL program is a sequence of rule firings. When two or more rules are firable, the selection of which rule to fire first is up to the runtime scheduler, which can use a nondeterministic scheduling policy, provided that firable rules with the highest priority are selected first. An EQL program is said to have reached a jked point when none of its rules are firable.

div.p: The state space S of an EQL program is the cartesian product of the domains of each of its variables. At each moment during an execution, the state of an EQL program is determined by the values of its variables at that instant. We also presented an algorithm to compute a bound on program's responsetime based on the two rule relations. div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Previous work in computing the response-time bounds for rule-based programs usually assumes nondeterministic choice when two or more rules are enabled. This assumption may result in overly pessimistic estimation of the response time when programmers deliberately exploit an a priori priority structure over the rules in conflict resolution. In this paper, we discuss how to get tighter bounds by taking rule-priority information into account. We have presented a bound-derivation algorithm, followed by its correctness proof. A response-time analyzer has been implemented to analyze programs whose potentialtrigger relations satisfy an acyclicity condition which seems to hold for most of the timecritical application programs that we have encountered. An analysis example is given to demonstrate the analysis process. Although we did not prove it in this paper, the input to the algorithm does not have to be the exact PT graph. It can be any supergraph of the PT graph, provided that no cycles are in the graph. This allows us to use approximation conditions in computing the potential-trigger relation, under the chance of getting looser bounds. The presented algorithm, which is es- sentially based on the spawn principle, does not use the detected suppression relation though. In a future paper we shall present an improved version based on the hybrid principle.

The target rule-based language in this paper, EQL, is designed to capture the subset of expert systems where the set of decision variables is fixed a priori. This seems to be the class of rule-based programs that are most commonly found in expert system applications that are truly time-critical, i.e., no more than a few milliseconds of response time is tolerable. The use of more general expert system programs with dynamically varying working memories for such time-critical applications is beyond the state-of-the-art, partially because currently, the application engineer has no tool to determine with any certainty whether "deliberation" is worth the time lost to taking immediate ac- tion. In future work, we shall extend the techniques in this paper to rule-based languages with dynamic working memories for the decision variables.

div.head: An analysis example
div.p: Based on the bound-derivation algorithm in the previous section and the approximation conditions presented in [ll], we implemented a response-time analyzer for EQL programs with acyclic PT graphs. To demonstrate the analysis process we present the analysis example of the following contrived EQL program.

The above output shows that, for example, to compute a weight bound for rule 2, in step 54 the analyzer picks rule 5 first between the two rules (rules 3 and 5) potentially triggered by rule 2. (Note that rule 5 has a higher priority than rule 3.) The analyzer then finds that rule 3 can also be included in the set Tp in step 56, and thus returns 5 as a weight bound of rule 2.

The above analysis takes only a fraction of a second on a Sparc 10 workstation. For comparison, without using the rule-priority information, the analyzer would report a bound of 18 firings for the program.
